Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

derivations.claim: Choose a nondegenerate closed rectangle $B$ containing $\operatorname{supp}f$. For every $z\in\mathbb C^2$, the integrand $x\mapsto f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot z}$ is continuous on $B$, so [F2] makes its real and imaginary parts Riemann integrable. It vanishes outside $\operatorname{supp}f$; hence enlarging $B$ changes the integral only by adding regions on which the integrand is zero. This proves existence and independence of the containing rectangle.

Fix $j\in\{1,2\}$, fix the other complex coordinate, and let $h\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$. By [F4], the coordinate difference quotient is the integral over $B$ of $f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot z}(e^{-2\pi i x_jh}-1)/h$. The coordinate $x_j$ is bounded on $B$; [F3] therefore makes $(e^{-2\pi i x_jh}-1)/h$ converge uniformly on $B$ to $-2\pi i x_j$ as $h\to0$. Multiplication by the fixed bounded continuous factor $f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot z}$ preserves uniform convergence, and [F4] passes the real and imaginary integrals to their limits. Thus the coordinate derivative exists and is the displayed integral. Since the other coordinate and the point were arbitrary, every coordinate slice is complex differentiable everywhere.

By [F5], each coordinate slice is entire. At real $z=\xi$, the defining integral is exactly the compact-support Fourier integral of [F1], so $F(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi)$. This proves all claims without using a Lebesgue/Riemann identification theorem or Countable Choice.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$, define $R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$, where the absolutely convergent integral is with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Here $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$ is the space of smooth complex functions for which every seminorm $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^2}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$, for multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$, is finite. The parameter $\theta$ is the unit normal to the line, so $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$ represent the same unoriented line. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Lebesgue integral in this definition agrees on compactly supported smooth inputs with the compact-support Riemann line integral, so the normalization is the same.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Fix a derivative multi-index $\beta$ and an integer $N\ge1$, and choose an integer $m\ge N$. Since $(1+|x|)^N\le(1+|x_1|)^m(1+|x_2|)^m$, expanding the right side and using the finite Schwartz seminorms in [F1] gives a finite $C_{\beta,N}(f)$ with $|\partial^\beta f(x)|\le C_{\beta,N}(f)(1+|x|)^{-N}$. For $x=s\theta+t\theta^\perp$, orthogonality gives $|x|=(s^2+t^2)^{1/2}\ge(|s|+|t|)/\sqrt2$, so the line integrand is bounded by a constant times $(1+|s|+|t|)^{-N}$. Taking $N>1$ makes this majorant integrable in $t$, proving absolute convergence.

Let $D_\theta=\theta\cdot\nabla$. The chain rule [F4] gives $\partial_s^k f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)=(D_\theta^k f)(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)$. Expanding $D_\theta^k$ gives finitely many partial derivatives with coefficients bounded uniformly for $\theta\in S^1$. For the target decay order $N$, apply step 1.1 with spatial decay order $N+2$ to each such derivative. Integrating $(1+|s|+|t|)^{-N-2}$ in $t$ gives $\left|\int_{\mathbb R}(D_\theta^k f)(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt\right|\le C'_{k,N}(1+|s|)^{-N-1}\le C'_{k,N}(1+|s|)^{-N}$, uniformly in $\theta$ and $s$.

Fix $s_0\in\mathbb R$ and a bounded open interval $I$ containing $s_0$. For each $k\ge0$, set $g_k(t,s)=(D_\theta^k f)(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)$. Every slice $g_k(\cdot,s)$ is integrable by step 1.1; it is differentiable in $s$ with derivative $g_{k+1}$ by [F4], and this derivative is measurable. Step 1.1 with spatial decay order $3$ bounds $|g_{k+1}(t,s)|\le C(1+|t|)^{-3}$ uniformly for $s\in I$, an integrable majorant. Thus [F3] proves $\frac{d}{ds}\int g_k(t,s)\,dt=\int g_{k+1}(t,s)\,dt$. To see each resulting derivative is continuous, if $s=s'$ the difference is zero; otherwise apply [F5] to real and imaginary parts on the segment joining $s$ and $s'$. The same majorant gives $|g_k(t,s)-g_k(t,s')|\le C|s-s'|(1+|t|)^{-3}$, and integration proves local continuity. Repeating for all $k$ and using the estimates in step 2.1 shows the offset function is Schwartz.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Choose $R>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq\overline B_R(0)$. If $|t|>R$, then $|s\theta+t\theta^\perp|\ge|t|>R$ and the integrand in [F1] is zero. On any compact set of $(\theta,s)$, uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact image of $(s,\theta,t)$ for $|t|\le R$ shows that the line integrals vary continuously: the difference of two such integrals is at most $2R$ times the uniform difference of their integrands. Hence the data function is continuous and measurable.

Put $D=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)$ and $T_{\theta,s}=\{t\in\mathbb R:s\theta+t\theta^\perp\in\Omega\}$. Any two points of $T_{\theta,s}$ differ by at most $D$, so this open set is contained in an interval of length at most $D$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F2] on $T_{\theta,s}$, where the constant function $1$ has squared integral at most $D$, gives $|R_{\mathcal S}f(\theta,s)|^2\le D\int_{\mathbb R}|f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|^2\,dt$.

The function $(\theta,s,t)\mapsto|f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|^2$ is bounded and vanishes unless $|s|,|t|\le R$, so it is integrable on the finite-measure set $\Theta\times[-R,R]^2$. Apply [F4] to exchange the iterated integrals, and for each $\theta$ apply [F3] to the orthogonal diffeomorphism $(s,t)\mapsto s\theta+t\theta^\perp$, whose absolute Jacobian is one. This gives $\int_\Theta\int_{\mathbb R^2}|f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|^2\,ds\,dt\,d\theta=|\Theta|\,\|f\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. Integrating step 1.2 yields the claimed bound and square-integrability.

$$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta).$$

Let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ and, for $z=(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2$, define $F(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(x)e^{-2\pi i(x_1z_1+x_2z_2)}\,dx$ using the compact-support Riemann integral on any rectangle containing $\operatorname{supp}f$. This value is independent of the containing rectangle. Each coordinate slice of $F$ is entire, with $\frac{\partial F}{\partial z_j}(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}(-2\pi ix_j)f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot z}\,dx$ for $j=1,2$, and the restriction of $F$ to $\mathbb R^2$ is the compact-support Fourier transform in the stated line-normal convention. The proof uses no Countable Choice.

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain (A complex domain is a nonempty connected open subset of $\mathbb C$), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.
Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $A\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$ be a unital subalgebra which separates points. Then $A$ is dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$ for the supremum metric.

derivations.claim: The hypothesis and the compact-support Fourier-slice identity [F2] give $\widehat f(\sigma\theta)=0$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$. By [F1], this includes the nonempty open positive-radius sector generated by $J$; choose a product of open real intervals $I_1\times I_2$ inside that sector. For each real $\xi_2\in I_2$, the entire function $z_1\mapsto\widehat f(z_1,\xi_2)$ vanishes on $I_1$, so [F5] makes it zero for every complex $z_1$. Then for every real $\xi_1$ the entire second-coordinate slice vanishes on $I_2$, and [F5] makes it zero everywhere. Thus $\widehat f$ vanishes on all of $\mathbb R^2$.

Let $K=\operatorname{supp}f$. If $K=\varnothing$, then $f=0$. Otherwise, fix a rectangle $B$ whose interior contains $K$ and interpret all integrals below as compact-support Riemann integrals over $B$. Repeated use of the coordinate derivative formula in [F3] shows $\int_B x^\alpha f(x)\,dx=0$ for every multi-index $\alpha$, since all real-frequency derivatives of $\widehat f$ vanish at the origin. The real polynomials restricted to $K$ form a unital subalgebra separating points, because the coordinate functions distinguish distinct points. By [F6], approximate $\operatorname{Re}\overline f$ and $\operatorname{Im}\overline f$ uniformly on $K$ by real polynomials; combine these approximations into complex polynomials $p_j$. Every moment is zero, so $\int_Bfp_j=0$. Also $f=0$ outside $K$, so $\int_B|f|^2=\left|\int_Bf(\overline f-p_j)\right|\le\sqrt2\,\operatorname{vol}(B)\|f\|_{C(B)}\|p_j-\overline f\|_{C(K)}\to0$, using the real Riemann integral bound [F4] on both components. If $f$ were nonzero at a point, continuity would bound $|f|^2$ below by a positive number on a nondegenerate box inside $B$, forcing its nonnegative Riemann integral to be positive. Thus $f=0$ everywhere. This proof uses neither Fourier inversion nor Countable Choice.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force

lemma is available.

$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
(Maximum and minimum of a set, Every nonempty finite set of reals has a maximum and a minimum). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.
